title: Jethro's advice (Exodus 18:13–27)
hookLine: his father-in-law says: you'll wear yourself out, share the load

lines: AN OLD MAN WATCHES ALL DAY.
cards: A line has formed outside a tent in the desert. It started at sunrise. By noon it snakes past the cooking fires.
A man wants to know whose goat it really was. Two cousins are fighting over a well. A widow has a complaint about her neighbor's fence.
At the front, on a seat, one man hears every case himself: Moses. The people stand there, the text says, from the morning until the evening.
At the back, an older man who has just arrived watches the whole day: Moses' father-in-law, Jethro, a priest from Midian. When the long day is over, he says what he has seen.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "The thing that thou doest is not good." Blunt.
Then the reason: "thou art not able to perform it thyself alone." He's not calling Moses lazy or proud. He's saying this will wear him out, and the people too, standing in that line all day.
Then a plan. Keep the hard cases, and the work of teaching the people the way.

teach.h: ABLE PEOPLE OVER TENS AND FIFTIES.
teach.b: Find able people to judge the everyday ones, over groups of a thousand, a hundred, fifty and ten: people who fear God, who tell the truth, who hate a bribe. Moses listens, and does exactly what his father-in-law says.
Notice who gave the advice. Jethro isn't an Israelite.

teach.h: THE ADVICE CAME FROM AN OUTSIDER.
teach.b: He's a priest of Midian, an outsider, who earlier in the chapter hears the whole story of the rescue from Egypt and blesses God for it.
The Bible lets a foreign father-in-law teach the great leader about leadership, and doesn't seem embarrassed at all.
Jewish tradition honors him: the weekly Torah reading that contains the Ten Commandments is named Yitro, after Jethro. Christians read this chapter in many ways.
Some churches point to it when they choose elders or deacons. Others hear in it permission to ask for help.

teach.h: THOU ART NOT ABLE TO PERFORM IT THYSELF ALONE.
teach.b: Moses, who has talked with God at a burning bush, still can't carry a whole people alone.
That's been the shape of the week: a night of remembering, a hurried exit, a sea, a song, manna, tired arms held up, and now the load shared.

how: Some churches point to Exodus 18 when they appoint elders, deacons or lay leaders to share the work of a congregation, and some pastors cite Jethro's advice when talking about burnout and shared ministry.

o: share the load: let able people judge small cases
leave Egypt behind and judge by Midian's own laws
pray longer before deciding each hard case

games.q: who's who at the tent — tap the pairs.
p: a priest of Midian, Moses' father-in-law
the Torah reading named for Jethro

s: he was a priest of Midian, an outsider, and Moses took his advice.
Moses kept the hardest cases for himself
the everyday cases went to others; the hard ones still came to Moses.
he said the opposite: Moses was doing too much, and it would wear everyone out.

games.q: you're Moses. you've talked with God, led a people through the sea, and now your father-in-law says you're doing it wrong. what do you do?
o: thank him, and keep doing it your way.
listen, and do what he says.
ask God to send more hours in the day.
games.why: Moses listens and does everything Jethro said. the great leader takes advice from an outsider, and the text tells it without embarrassment.

practice: Picture your own line outside the tent, everything that's waiting on you this week, and look down it for one thing somebody else could do, not badly, just differently than you would. Notice what makes it hard to let go.
If you pray, you can ask for the Jethro in your life to speak up.

wordCard.voice: Jethro's advice. A father-in-law from Midian watches Moses judge alone from morning to evening and says: share the load, or it will wear you out.

orig.note: Hebrew: Jethro's name. Jewish tradition names the Torah reading with the Ten Commandments after him.

carryVoice: Your line: you can't do it alone. And that's week fifty-six: Passover, haste, the sea, a tambourine, manna, tired arms, and Jethro.
